label: Model Selection & Design Considerations — Part A

questions.scenario: A team is evaluating two models for a product recommendation engine. Model X achieves 98.2% accuracy at $45,000/month in compute. Model Y achieves 97.4% accuracy at $4,500/month. The business requirement specifies a minimum accuracy threshold of 95%.
questions.stem: Which factor should be the PRIMARY driver of their model selection decision?

options.text: The absolute accuracy difference of 0.8% between the two models
The total number of parameters in each model
Which model was released more recently
Whether the accuracy improvement justifies a 10x increase in operational cost given both exceed the requirement

explanation.correct: When both models exceed the stated requirement (95%), the decision becomes a cost-performance tradeoff. A 0.8% accuracy gain costing 10x more may not deliver proportional business value, making cost-performance balance the primary factor.

distractors.A: Absolute accuracy difference alone is insufficient for decision-making without considering what that improvement costs and whether it produces meaningful business impact.
distractors.B: Parameter count influences inference cost and latency but is not the primary selection criterion when concrete accuracy and cost data are already available.
distractors.C: Release date does not determine model suitability. Older models may outperform newer ones for specific tasks.

questions.scenario: An autonomous drone navigation system requires obstacle detection decisions within 15ms. The engineering team has narrowed candidates to three models with inference times of 8ms, 14ms, and 22ms respectively.
questions.stem: Why should the 22ms model be eliminated regardless of its accuracy advantage?

options.text: Models with higher accuracy always consume more memory than available on drones
Longer inference times reduce training efficiency for future model updates
The model cannot produce predictions within the latency constraint required for safe real-time operation
Higher-latency models are incompatible with edge deployment hardware

explanation.correct: When a system requires real-time decisions within a hard latency constraint (15ms), any model exceeding that threshold cannot meet the functional requirement regardless of how accurate it is — safety demands timely predictions.

distractors.A: Memory and accuracy do not have a direct causal relationship. Many accurate models are optimized for constrained environments.
distractors.B: Training efficiency is unrelated to inference latency constraints. The issue is real-time prediction speed, not future training.
distractors.D: Latency is not inherently tied to hardware compatibility. A model can be hardware-compatible yet still too slow for the application's timing needs.

questions.stem: A model with 175 billion parameters outperforms a 7 billion parameter model on benchmark tests. Which tradeoff is MOST directly introduced by choosing the larger model?

options.text: Reduced training data requirements since larger models generalize from fewer examples
Increased explainability because more parameters capture clearer decision boundaries
Higher computational cost and reduced ability to explain why the model produces specific outputs
Lower risk of bias since more parameters dilute individual data point influence

explanation.correct: Greater model complexity increases computational requirements (cost, memory, inference time) while simultaneously reducing interpretability — more parameters make it harder to trace how inputs lead to outputs.

distractors.A: Larger models still benefit from more data. While they may generalize better, they do not eliminate data requirements.
distractors.B: More parameters create more opaque decision processes, not clearer ones. Interpretability decreases with complexity.
distractors.D: Parameter count does not reduce bias. Bias originates from training data distributions, not model size.

questions.scenario: A financial regulator requires that a bank's loan approval system provide a complete mathematical audit trail showing exactly how each input variable contributed to the approval decision.
questions.stem: Which approach satisfies this regulatory requirement?

options.text: Deploy a foundation model with SHAP explanations attached to each prediction
Use a logistic regression or decision tree model where coefficients and splits are directly auditable
Fine-tune a large language model on historical loan decisions to learn the approval logic
Use a foundation model and log all attention weights as the audit trail

explanation.correct: Logistic regression coefficients and decision tree splits provide exact mathematical relationships between inputs and outputs — true interpretability where every decision step is traceable through formulas.

distractors.A: SHAP provides post-hoc approximations of feature importance, not complete mathematical audit trails. It explains behavior without revealing exact internal mechanics.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning an LLM would create a black-box system. Learning from historical decisions does not produce auditable mathematical logic.
distractors.D: Attention weights show where the model focuses but do not constitute a mathematical audit trail of how variable values produce the final decision.

questions.scenario: A fraud detection model processes 10,000 transactions daily. Only 15 are typically fraudulent. The model correctly identifies 9,985 legitimate transactions and 10 of the 15 fraudulent ones, reporting 99.5% accuracy.
questions.stem: Why is this accuracy figure misleading for evaluating the model's effectiveness?

options.text: Accuracy should only be calculated on weekly aggregates, not daily transactions
A model predicting every transaction as legitimate would achieve 99.85% accuracy, making the metric unreliable for imbalanced classes
Accuracy cannot be applied to binary classification problems with numerical inputs
The sample size of 10,000 is too small for accuracy to be statistically valid

explanation.correct: With 15/10,000 positive cases, a naive model predicting all transactions as legitimate achieves 99.85% accuracy. The actual model's 99.5% accuracy obscures that it missed 5 fraudulent transactions — precision and recall better capture performance on the minority class.

distractors.A: Aggregation period does not fix the fundamental problem of class imbalance distorting accuracy as a metric.
distractors.C: Accuracy applies to any classification problem. The issue is class imbalance making it misleading, not input data types.
distractors.D: 10,000 samples is statistically sufficient. The problem is the metric's inability to reflect minority-class performance.

questions.stem: A team is selecting a pre-trained model for a multilingual customer service application that must handle text and image inputs with sub-second response times. Which criteria are MOST relevant to this selection? (Select THREE)

options.text: Support for the required input modalities and target languages
Inference latency under production load conditions
Licensing terms that permit commercial deployment
Whether the model was trained using PyTorch or TensorFlow
The total size of the model's training dataset in terabytes
The number of research papers citing the model

explanation.correct: Modality and language support determines functional fit, inference latency determines whether sub-second SLAs can be met, and licensing determines whether commercial use is legally permitted — all are blocking criteria.

distractors.D: The original training framework matters for fine-tuning compatibility but most models can be served through framework-agnostic inference runtimes.
distractors.E: Training dataset size contributes to model quality but is already reflected in benchmark performance. It is not a direct selection criterion.
distractors.F: Citation count indicates research impact but does not guarantee the model meets specific latency, modality, or licensing requirements.

questions.scenario: A medical imaging team needs to evaluate models for detecting tumors in X-rays. They need metrics that capture both the model's ability to find actual tumors and its tendency to flag healthy tissue as abnormal.
questions.stem: Which metrics directly address both of these evaluation needs? (Select THREE)

options.text: Recall — measures the proportion of actual tumors correctly identified
Precision — measures the proportion of flagged cases that are actual tumors
F1 score — balances precision and recall into a single metric
Perplexity — measures how well the model predicts the next token
BLEU — measures translation quality against references
Training loss — measures how well the model fits its training data

explanation.correct: Recall captures tumor detection rate (sensitivity), precision captures false alarm rate, and F1 balances both. Together they directly address finding tumors (recall) and avoiding false positives (precision).

distractors.D: Perplexity evaluates language model fluency, not classification performance on medical imaging tasks.
distractors.E: BLEU evaluates text translation quality by comparing to reference translations. It is irrelevant to image classification.
distractors.F: Training loss indicates training convergence but does not directly measure the specific behaviors requested — it could be low while the model still misses tumors.

questions.scenario: A healthcare startup is evaluating a pre-trained model from an open-source repository for patient symptom triage. Their CTO asks the engineering lead to verify readiness before integration.
questions.stem: Which verifications should the engineering lead perform before adopting this model? (Select THREE)

options.text: Confirm the license permits commercial use in healthcare applications
Check for documented known issues, limitations, and when the model was last maintained
Verify compatibility with their existing inference framework and deployment environment
Confirm the model has been starred by at least 1,000 GitHub users
Verify the model creators have medical degrees
Check that the model repository has a custom domain name

explanation.correct: License verification prevents legal risk, documentation of issues/maintenance status reveals reliability, and framework compatibility ensures the model can actually be deployed in their environment.

distractors.D: Stars indicate popularity but not quality, safety, or fitness for regulated healthcare applications.
distractors.E: Model creators need ML expertise, not medical degrees. Clinical validation is a separate process from model evaluation.
distractors.F: Repository domain names are cosmetic and have no bearing on model quality or safety.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe the relationship between interpretability and explainability in machine learning? (Select TWO)

options.text: Interpretability means understanding the model's internal mechanics through coefficients, weights, or decision rules
Explainability approximates a complex model's behavior locally using a simpler, interpretable surrogate model
Explainability requires full access to the model's source code and training data
Interpretable models always achieve higher accuracy than non-interpretable models
A model can be both fully interpretable and have billions of parameters

explanation.correct: Interpretability provides direct understanding of internal mechanics (e.g., linear regression coefficients). Explainability treats the model as a black box and approximates its behavior locally with simpler models — different approaches to understanding predictions.

distractors.C: Explainability methods like LIME and SHAP work by observing input-output behavior. They do not require source code or training data access.
distractors.D: Interpretability and accuracy often have an inverse relationship — simpler interpretable models typically sacrifice some accuracy.
distractors.E: Billions of parameters create computational paths too complex for human interpretation. True interpretability requires tractable model structures.

questions.stem: Beyond performance metrics, which factors should be evaluated when selecting a pre-trained model for production deployment? (Select TWO)

options.text: Potential biases inherited from the model's training data that could produce unfair outputs
Customization flexibility such as adding task-specific layers or adjusting the output space
The geographic timezone of the model's training compute cluster
Whether the model name follows a consistent naming convention with other company models
The total number of contributors to the model's repository

explanation.correct: Training data biases can produce discriminatory outputs in production, creating ethical and legal risk. Customization flexibility determines whether the model can be adapted to specific requirements without starting from scratch.

distractors.C: Training location has no impact on model behavior or suitability. Performance and capabilities are what matter.
distractors.D: Naming conventions are organizational preferences with no impact on model quality or fitness.
distractors.E: Contributor count indicates community activity but does not directly predict model suitability for a specific production use case.

questions.scenario: A startup with $2,000/month compute budget needs an image classification model for their mobile app. They find a state-of-the-art model achieving 99.1% accuracy requiring $18,000/month in inference costs, and a distilled variant achieving 96.8% at $1,800/month.
questions.stem: Which model selection principle applies here?

options.text: Always choose the highest-accuracy model and seek additional funding to cover costs
Deploy both models and route traffic based on query complexity
Reject both models and build a custom model from scratch to reduce ongoing costs
Select the distilled variant since it meets accuracy needs within budget constraints, balancing performance against available resources

explanation.correct: Model selection requires balancing performance against resource constraints. The distilled variant delivers strong accuracy (96.8%) within the budget, demonstrating that the right model fits both technical and financial requirements.

distractors.A: Ignoring budget constraints is not a viable strategy. Model selection must account for financial sustainability.
distractors.B: Routing adds infrastructure complexity and the expensive model still exceeds budget. This doesn't solve the constraint.
distractors.C: Building from scratch requires far more than $2,000/month in development costs and typically produces worse results than leveraging pre-trained models.

questions.scenario: A conversational AI team measures their current model at 2.3 seconds per response. User research shows that engagement drops 40% when responses exceed 1.5 seconds. The team considers three optimization paths: model distillation, quantization, or switching to a smaller architecture.
questions.stem: What does this scenario illustrate about model selection for interactive applications?

options.text: Inference speed requirements are determined by user experience thresholds, not just technical capabilities
All three optimization paths will produce identical latency improvements
User engagement is unrelated to response latency in conversational AI
The only solution is to increase hardware resources rather than change the model

explanation.correct: Latency requirements emerge from application context — here, user engagement data defines the acceptable threshold (1.5s). Model selection must satisfy these application-driven constraints, not just optimize for accuracy.

distractors.B: Distillation, quantization, and architecture changes produce different latency-accuracy tradeoffs. Each has distinct characteristics.
distractors.C: The scenario explicitly shows a 40% engagement drop tied to latency. Response speed directly impacts user experience.
distractors.D: Hardware scaling is one option but not the only one. Model-level optimizations (distillation, quantization, smaller architectures) can also meet latency targets.

questions.scenario: A manufacturing company needs AI to analyze defective products using photos from assembly lines, audio recordings of machine vibrations, and maintenance logs written in English, Mandarin, and German.
questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY architectural consideration for this use case?

options.text: Selecting a single large language model and converting all inputs to text descriptions
Using separate specialized models for each modality — one team cannot manage multimodal systems
Prioritizing the text modality since maintenance logs contain the most actionable information
Choosing models that support the required modalities and languages, potentially using ensemble approaches to combine specialized capabilities

explanation.correct: Multi-modal requirements demand models supporting each needed modality (image, audio, text) with multilingual capability. Ensemble methods can combine specialized models for better performance than forcing a single model to handle everything.

distractors.A: Converting images and audio to text loses critical information (visual defect patterns, vibration frequencies) that text cannot capture.
distractors.B: Multi-modal systems are standard practice. The concern is selecting appropriate models for each modality, not avoiding the architecture entirely.
distractors.C: Arbitrarily prioritizing one modality ignores valuable signals from others. Defect detection may require correlating visual, audio, and text data.

questions.scenario: A search engine team evaluates their ranking model. They need a metric that captures whether relevant results appear at the top of the search results list, not just whether they appear somewhere.
questions.stem: Which metric is most appropriate for evaluating ranked retrieval quality?

options.text: Accuracy — the percentage of queries that return at least one correct result
Mean Average Precision (MAP) — measures precision at each rank position where relevant documents are retrieved
Recall — the proportion of all relevant documents that appear anywhere in results
F1 score — the harmonic mean of precision and recall across all results

explanation.correct: MAP evaluates precision at each rank position where a relevant result appears, directly measuring whether relevant results are ranked higher. It rewards models that place relevant documents at the top of results.

distractors.A: Accuracy only measures presence/absence. It doesn't capture whether relevant results appear at position 1 vs position 100.
distractors.C: Recall measures coverage but is position-agnostic. A system returning all relevant results at the bottom of the page scores well on recall but poorly on ranking quality.
distractors.D: F1 balances precision and recall without considering rank position. It treats a result at position 1 identically to one at position 50.

questions.scenario: A data science team deploys a deep neural network for credit scoring. Regulators ask the team to explain why a specific applicant was denied. The team uses LIME to generate a local explanation showing which features most influenced the denial.
questions.stem: What type of understanding does this LIME explanation provide?

options.text: Full interpretability — the team now understands exactly how every neuron contributed to the decision
Explainability — an approximation of the model's behavior for this specific prediction using a simpler surrogate
Transparency — the model's internal decision process is now fully visible and auditable
Reproducibility — the same explanation will be generated for every applicant regardless of their features

explanation.correct: LIME provides explainability by approximating the black-box model locally with a simpler interpretable model. It describes behavior for a specific prediction without revealing the actual internal mechanics.

distractors.A: LIME does not expose internal neuron-level mechanics. It builds a local surrogate approximation — an explanation, not full interpretability.
distractors.C: The deep neural network remains a black box. LIME provides an external approximation, not transparency into the model's actual decision process.
distractors.D: LIME generates different explanations for different inputs because it approximates local behavior. Each prediction gets its own local explanation.

questions.scenario: An engineering team presents their CTO with two architecture options: a 7B parameter model and a 70B parameter model. Both are candidates for a customer-facing product.
questions.stem: What are direct consequences of choosing the 70B parameter model over the 7B? (Select TWO)

options.text: Higher computational cost for both training and inference due to processing more parameters
Reduced ability to explain model decisions to customers or auditors
Guaranteed elimination of hallucinations due to broader knowledge
Automatic compliance with data privacy regulations
Faster inference speed due to more efficient parameter utilization

explanation.correct: More parameters directly increase computational requirements (more multiplications per forward pass) and reduce interpretability (more complex decision paths that cannot be traced by humans).

distractors.C: Larger models reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations. They can still generate plausible-sounding incorrect content on topics with sparse training data.
distractors.D: Model size has no relationship to regulatory compliance. Compliance requires specific data handling practices regardless of architecture.
distractors.E: More parameters generally increase inference time because more computations are required per forward pass. Larger models are slower, not faster.

questions.scenario: An AI product team is building a system that must process customer reviews (text), product photos (images), and support call recordings (audio) to generate quality scores.
questions.stem: Which architectural considerations apply to this multi-modal system? (Select TWO)

options.text: Each modality requires a distinct embedding representation to capture its unique information structure
Ensemble methods can combine outputs from modality-specific models to produce better overall predictions than any single model
All modalities must be converted to the same embedding dimensionality before any processing can occur
A single transformer architecture can natively process all modalities without any modality-specific preprocessing
Multi-modal systems require separate inference endpoints that cannot share compute resources

explanation.correct: Different modalities encode fundamentally different information types requiring distinct embeddings (text uses token embeddings, images use patch/pixel embeddings, audio uses spectral embeddings). Ensemble approaches leverage specialized models' strengths for superior combined predictions.

distractors.C: While embeddings may eventually be projected to compatible spaces, they do not need identical dimensionality for processing. Cross-attention and projection layers handle dimension differences.
distractors.D: Even multi-modal transformers require modality-specific preprocessing (tokenizers for text, patch extraction for images, spectrogram conversion for audio).
distractors.E: Multi-modal models can share compute infrastructure. Separation is an architectural choice, not a technical requirement.

questions.scenario: A pharmaceutical company is adopting a pre-trained model from Hugging Face for clinical trial document analysis. Their compliance officer needs verification before approval.
questions.stem: What should the compliance officer verify before approving model adoption? (Select THREE)

options.text: The model license explicitly permits use in commercial pharmaceutical applications
Known limitations and failure modes are documented, especially for medical text
The model is compatible with the company's existing ML infrastructure and deployment pipelines
The model has more downloads than alternative models on the platform
The model's training code is written in the same programming language the company primarily uses
The model was trained by a company with pharmaceutical industry experience

explanation.correct: License compliance is mandatory for legal use, documented limitations inform risk assessment for regulated domains, and infrastructure compatibility ensures practical deployability. All three are blocking criteria.

distractors.D: Download count reflects popularity but not regulatory fitness, safety, or suitability for pharmaceutical applications.
distractors.E: Training code language is irrelevant to deployment. Models are served through inference runtimes independent of training implementation.
distractors.F: ML expertise matters more than industry background for model development. Clinical validation is separate from model creation.

questions.scenario: A machine learning engineer's CNN achieves 94% accuracy on image recognition while a logistic regression model achieves 72% on the same task. When asked to justify the more complex model, the engineer must explain the accuracy gap.
questions.stem: What fundamentally explains why the CNN outperforms logistic regression on this task?

options.text: CNNs exploit spatial hierarchies and local patterns in images through convolutional filters — structural properties that linear models cannot capture
Logistic regression was not given enough training time to converge on the same patterns
CNNs always outperform all simpler models on every possible task
Logistic regression requires more training data than CNNs to achieve comparable accuracy

explanation.correct: Different architectures have different strengths. CNNs are designed to detect spatial patterns through hierarchical convolutional filters — a capability absent from linear models that treat each pixel independently.

distractors.B: Logistic regression converges quickly due to its convex loss function. Additional training time cannot make it capture spatial hierarchies it architecturally cannot represent.
distractors.C: Simpler models outperform CNNs on tasks where spatial structure is irrelevant (e.g., tabular data with independent features). Architecture suitability depends on the task.
distractors.D: CNNs typically require more data than logistic regression due to having more parameters. The advantage is architectural suitability, not data efficiency.

questions.scenario: A product team must decide between using a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock or training a task-specific BERT classifier for sentiment analysis on product reviews.
questions.stem: What is the key architectural distinction that differentiates foundation models from task-specific models?

options.text: Foundation models require fine-tuning on labeled data before they can perform any task
Task-specific models are always larger and more capable than foundation models
Foundation models cannot be used for classification tasks like sentiment analysis
Foundation models are general-purpose models that can perform diverse tasks through prompting, while task-specific models are optimized for a single function

explanation.correct: Foundation models are trained on broad data to perform many tasks via prompts without task-specific training. Task-specific models are optimized for one function, potentially achieving higher accuracy on that task but lacking generalization.

distractors.A: Foundation models can perform tasks through zero-shot or few-shot prompting without any fine-tuning. Fine-tuning is optional for specialization.
distractors.B: Foundation models are typically much larger than task-specific models. A foundation model like Claude has far more parameters than a fine-tuned BERT classifier.
distractors.C: Foundation models readily perform classification including sentiment analysis through prompting. They handle the same tasks as specialized models plus many more.
